utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Mr. Ajie Buhron, who is from Indonesia, has been with my team since March of this year, and holds a masters in international law from the University of Groningen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Yes, Mr. Zec, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we talked about the fear that caused many non-Serbs to leave their homes. Before I play that radio broadcast, let me ask you about events in the neighbourhood of Sanski Most called Mahala. There is evidence before this Chamber that in late May 1992, Serb soldiers forced Mahala residents to gather at the training ground and then the area was shelled and non-Serb property was destroyed, following which thousands of unarmed non-Serbs were detained and many were killed. Do you recall this event, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During that period of time, I was not in the area, and that information is not accessible to me, and my statement probably would not be that reliable. It would actually be like that of all the citizens who live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then hear the broadcast now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is P00725, and we have provided the transcripts to the interpreters so this can be translated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... all the struggle and retaliation will be in vain. You're not capable of standing up to the forces of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the statement of the Serbian Armed Forces Command states. It adds, your resistance will force us to destroy and devastate your villages, which means that you will not be able to live with us in these territories. If you do want to go on living in these territories, accept cooperation, hand over all the weapons and military equipment and surrender to the Serbian authorities all the extremists who force you to fight. As long as one of you has a weapon, you risk the destruction of your houses and families ... weapons and hand them over to the public security station or the Crisis Staff. The roads are free, fire won't be opened until the deadline. The following villages have to hand over their" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I missed something but could we know what the date is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I said that yesterday. It's late May. It's most probably 27 May 1992. And as is going to be clear in this clip, it's after the events in Mahala and one of the -- there is also on this same page one reference that: Today we will do the same as we did in Mahala. So that's the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So this was the reality, Mr. Davidovic. We heard in this official statements words "as long as one of you has a weapon, you risk the destruction of your houses and families." And the destruction of Mahala was used as one example and the threat to non-Serbs as to what awaited them. This threat was effective and many non-Serbs left; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, as far as this radio clip is concerned, if I can call it that, I hardly listened to the radio then, as is the case today. I mostly read newspapers and watch TV. But never mind, I can still give my comment on the basis of what I heard just now. In view of all of, this you should probably put that question to the citizens of the other ethnicity, what their attitude was to what they had heard. From my point of view, I said in my statement that this fear of war was such that it compelled, inter alia, the population to leave, economic conditions and so on and so forth. In view of what happened in 1941, what happened in Sanski Most then, then there was fear of that, also what happened in 1995 in Sanski Most. I mean I really cannot give my comments with regard to how this affected citizens of the other ethnicity. I could only take action once they submitted requests to leave. This was probably under the authority of other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And to be clear, the translation stopped at one point because Mr. Karadzic interrupted, and at the end of this clip I wanted to play, it says: "We will be forced to act as we did with Mahala." So this was clear threat, knowing what happened in Mahala, that people would be feared of this; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that part. I'm saying that I worked at the end of 1993. That is to say, when the situation calmed down, I started working at the municipal administration, and I mean, there were these requests that were submitted then, when there were no more war operations in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's be clear. Yesterday, we talked about your role in the commission for relocation of population. You said that you were appointed to this commission towards the end of 1993 and before that you did not perform any function. That's what you said also now. And this is also at transcript page 44509, 44510. So this is your evidence before this Court; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't hold me on that, the date. The end of 1992, beginning of 1993, that part really, but I said after all of these war developments were over, and when the authorities of Sanski Most started functioning, I was a civil servant then, as I am now, and I received instructions from the Executive Board as the legitimate organ of government in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I'm trying to be clear here. I'm talking about commission for relocation of population. I asked you yesterday many questions about that and you told me were you in the commission as of end of 1993. So that's the date that you got at the commission and you were dealing with these issues from that period; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm talking about you and your role. You got on the commission late 1993. That's what you based your knowledge about these events; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission at the end of 1993, I think it was the commission that had to do with departures through the Republic of Croatia, and I think that the end of 1992, beginning of 1993, there was this other commission, and I did not play a very active part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And your active part was in late 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the representative of the centre for social welfare, in the work of these commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And when you talk about the work of the commission in paragraph 20 of your statement, this relates to the period when you were at the commission, late 1993 and after; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: When you say that the commission assisted people to move out by providing logistics such as transport, arranging contacts, documents, you were talking about the late 1993 and after; correct? That's your evidence before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is probably right. That's what it says. That's what's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: When you say that -- that you and the commission assisted citizens who wished to leave and who had expressed a wish to leave, you were referring to the period after late 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And when you say that nobody ever forced non-Serbs to move out, you were referring again to late 1993 and after; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the entire period, to the best of my knowledge, as regards that entire period, and on the basis of the information that I had from the persons who were leaving Sanski Most, regardless of whether these were members of the other ethnicity or whether they were ethnic Serbs. Probably in that period of time, I, who did not have a job, did not have any income whatsoever, I probably would have left if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the end of your sentence. Can you just repeat that last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying, bearing in mind the situation that prevailed at the time, and the fact that I was jobless and so on, I said that if I had somewhere to go, I probably would have left Sanski Most too. I would have gone to a better destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I asked you yesterday about massive destruction, about statements of the SDS leader to expel people. We talked about Mahala. I played for you this radio -- the threats over the radio and you say you had no any knowledge about it; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, if you were in my place, and if you lived 20 kilometres away from that place, and if you were involved in agriculture and if you were helping your parents with their work, you really would not have time to deal with all of these things. I tried to survive at that time and to help my parents till the land. Really, everything was aimed in that direction. And then once conditions were created, of course, I asked to continue working at the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's talk about a little bit different topic. Let's talk about dismissals of non-Serbs from their employment. It is correct, is it, that in May 1992, non-Serbs were dismissed and -- from their employment and Serbs took their positions; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this word, "dismissals," no, they did not show up for work. Members of other ethnicities. And many Serbs were away too, so that is why I was asked to work in the municipality of Sanski Most and to continue doing the work that I had done before I lost my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 256334 and these are minutes of the third session of the Municipal Assembly from May 1992. Can we have last page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At the end of the document, we see your name. So you took notes of this session; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have -- can we have page 4 of the English, page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this session discusses appointments to various posts in the municipality. And if we see item number 14, in item number 14, it refers to the appointment of Veso Majkic to the position of acting director of the post office. Can you confirm that Veso Majkic is a Serb name?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a Serb name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Before May 1992, this post was occupied by a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Probably. But I cannot remember now. I'm not sure but probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Item number 15 refers to the appointment of Bosko Grubisa to the position of the acting director of the health centre. He replaced Dr. Enes Sabanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Enes Sabanovic did something. Possibly he was a director and then, yes, in that period, Grubisa was appointed acting head of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Item number 16 refers to the appointment of Mile Cucak to the acting director of the fire house. He replaced a Croat, Nikola Kosoric; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile, yes, Mile Cucak came, yes. Well, I cannot say for sure. If that's the information there, well, yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Judge Nedzad Muhic, president of the municipal magistrate's court, was replaced by a Serb judge; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Nedzad Muhic was president of the misdemeanours court, not the basic court. I think that Adil Draganovic was president of the basic court. Maybe I'm making a mistake, but I think that he was a misdemeanours judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Regardless, both these people that you just mentioned were replaced by Serb judges; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Top positions, yes, presidents of these courts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Judge Muhic died in an overcrowded truck full of prisoners on the way to Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that you don't know anything, didn't hear anything, about the fate of this once-prominent judge?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just read about something in a book. I think it was a man from Kljuc who wrote about Sanski Most. In that period of time, I really didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to Judge Muhic, I refer to P718, page 25; P3634, pages 61-62; P3329, page 57; P3649; and P4853, page 48. And I would like to tender this document that we were looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6547, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's talk about the changes in the structure of the Sanski Most population from 1992 to 1993. It is correct, is it, that in 1993, there were about 4.000 Muslims and about 1.000 Croats left in Sanski Most, reduced from about 28.000 of Muslims and about 4.300 Croats before the conflict began? You know this; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I don't know who did the counting but these are probably figures from the census. This other part, 1991. As for the Muslims and Croats in Sanski Most. I know for sure because I was in the centre for social welfare and I coordinated humanitarian aid, a considerable number of Muslims, and I think Croats too, lived in Sanski Most in this period of time as well. And indeed, they continued to move out in 1994 and 1995 and a considerable number stayed on in Sanski Most after 1995, but I don't know the exact figures. I know that - how do I put this? - there were many in town when humanitarian aid was being distributed, and also in the Bliha Valley and Caplje and Poljak and Sekovici and Skrljevita in the direction of Banja Luka. I mean, I really cannot say which number is involved, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you're repeating more or less what you said in your statement. And please be aware that there are people who are translating what you're saying. You have to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- 25640. This is a census from Sanski Most made in 1993. And if we can have a look at e-court page in B/C/S and page 6 of the English, here we see an overview of the population structure in Sanski Most from 1990 -- 1961 to 1993. And in 1993, there were 4.390 Muslims and 1.247 Croats in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you knew this at the time, Mr. Davidovic; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I mean, it's hard to memorise figures, and I mean, this number -- well, I told you that I saw people but it's hard for me to say anything about the figure. I cannot confirm or deny it. After 20 years, it is very difficult to remember. I took part in the census commission in 1991 and I cannot remember the exact figures that were published, let alone this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you participated, as you say, in 1991 census, but you also participated in production of this census, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. In the organisation of the census, given my -- my experience, I participated in the organisation and ensured that the census was carried out in a correct manner, the census that was performed during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25642?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you look at the decision on the left top corner, it's decision appointing you to the commission and you were a member of the municipal commission for conducting this 1993 census that we just saw; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender these two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 25640 receives Exhibit Number P6548. 65 ter number 25642 receives Exhibit Number P6549, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you knew, and as this Chamber also knows, this reduction in the numbers of non-Serbs was required because Sanski Most had to be a Serbian town. P02657. That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't participate in those actions, and I really have to say that you're not putting the question to the right person. I did my work, the work that the organs of power had asked me to do. I carried out the census. You can see that this was all done legally. There was an overview of the situation. As for the causes and the effects of that, well, I wasn't competent to comment on that. It wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zec. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellencies. Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the video we saw, in the video excerpt, mention was made of numerous villages. Did some of those villages hand over their weapons, according to the information you have?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The witness testified that he has no idea what was going on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, Mr. President, this is a recurring objection that I think needs to be dealt with. The Prosecution constantly asks witnesses about what they say that they don't know about and puts things to them that either contradict or confirm other parts of their evidence, so there is no -- simply because the witness has at one point said he didn't know anything about an event doesn't mean that Dr. Karadzic can't put some information to him to see whether or not the witness is able to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that question not very leading, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a very legitimate objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, your Excellencies. Thank you. Could the witness be shown 65 ter document 04898?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You just told Mr. Karadzic to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he's moving on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Before even putting a document to a witness, he's supposed to ask some non-leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, where were you born, where did you live, and where did you spend the period during which you were unemployed?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in Bosanski Milanovac, a village which is between 15 and 20 kilometres from Sanski Most. That is where I lived during that period of time, at the beginning of 1992, at the end of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see this document, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the last exhibit, we saw that there were 4.300-odd Muslims. Where did they mostly live at the time? Were the villages where there were Muslims or did they only live in small places?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some lived in towns but there were also entire Muslim villages in the valley of the Bliha river, that's Husinovci, Donji/Gornji Kamengrad. Many of them worked in the coal mine. Many of them -- most of them worked there all the time. In the valley of the Sana river, there was Caplja and Tomina in the direction of Kljuc. And these -- amongst these Croats there was a Polish man from Skrljevita and Sehovici in the direction of Banja Luka. That's where they were in the majority, and they remained to live there, the Muslims who were on the census and Croats remained to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber what the difference is between those villages and Hrustovo, for example, which is where there was a crisis and fighting?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hrustovo, after that crisis, remained uninhabited, whereas these villages, under the circumstances, were organised in a certain way and they worked to the extent that that was possible given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you use this map to show us where your village is located, Milanovac, Bosanski Milanovac?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Jovici, that's part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you mark it with the letters B and M?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's a group of villages, of hamlets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, based on the surnames, Davidovici, Jovici, Milovici, and so on and so forth. Because that's why the map was made, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you use a -- could you draw a line under some of these villages where these Muslim people lived and worked or could you draw a circle around the names of these villages?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be here. It's here in this area. I've also marked the location of the river.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked not to mumble as the interpreter cannot understand what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for Tomina?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is this part towards Kljuc, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up as the interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was here at the river of Sana and the road towards Kljuc. That's where it is. Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please write down the date -- and towards the north, in fact, I apologise, Marina is Serbian and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm wondering, Mr. Karadzic, how this could assist the Chamber in any way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, your Excellencies, have a look towards the town itself, there are some Muslim villages that no one touched. So we want to determine why Hrustovo was treated differently, and Tomina and Kamengrad and so on and so forth were treated in a different manner. What's the basis for this difference in treatment? Is it faith or something else? That's essential for me, given my understanding of the indictment. If the policy was to remove them, if that is what the system was, why weren't they removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking about your case but how this map marking will assist your case? That was my question. Very well. Could you date -- put the date, which is 5th of December, 2013, and your signature, wherever you like, as you please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 5th. I have a better or more legible map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will assign a new number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number D4168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 85 of yesterday's transcript, Prosecution exhibit was shown, P6545. You were suggested as a candidate for the head of the police station and my approval was asked. Did I give my approval?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three candidates, and in terms of their rank, because of the system of ranking, I didn't get that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the case when some of the Muslims or the Croats had to pack up and leave Sanski Most? Were they forced to do so by the authorities, not because of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information. I have no knowledge of such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the Croatian villages in Sanski Most in which the Croats had remained and continued to work, go to school, these things were paid for by the municipality and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I made markings on the map, I said that there was this area of Molja [phoen] -- Poljak and Skrljevita where this was the case. Poljak was nearer to the town and that's where children went to school, and Skrljevita is nearer to the municipality. The municipality found means for the children who were far away from the town to also go to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in Sanski Most, was there a sort of market day? Did the Muslims and Croats go there to Sanski Most once a week?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Monday was market day in Sanski Most and on that day it was possible to see Muslims and Croats, and that market was in the very centre of town. There are various types of goods there, and livestock would also be sold and bought then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Davidovic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for treating me fairly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a brief submission before the next witness comes in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And if we could move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kalabic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Kalabic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your answer -- your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence except and save the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we please make pauses between questions and answers and speak slowly, but you aren't someone who speaks very fast. Did you give my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D9594?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see your statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I read the statement and I signed it, but I have to say that when I went through the statement, I noticed that there was a mistake that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just show the witness the last page so that he can see and identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now help us and tell us which paragraph is concerned? Do you have the printed statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: No. I don't. If we could scroll back a little, I can find the mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Chamber make it possible for the witness to have a hard copy of his statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we print it out, unless you have it with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, could it please be printed out in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told the court deputy is not able to print out from the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can do it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at it and tell us which paragraph the mistake appears in? Mr. Kalabic, was the mistake perhaps corrected in the course of the proofing?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it but I can't find the mistake that I noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, if you could tell us what it is about, then Mr. Karadzic can locate the paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It had to do with the Sanica and Biljani area, Marko Adamovic was mentioned as a name. The name should have been Marko Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph 18?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellency, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Will you pose a question to the witness about this? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, does it say it's Adamovic in the adjudicated facts but you know that it was someone else or --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: In the statement I gave, I said the person concerned was Marko Samardzija, but I later noticed that it says "Marko Adamovic." This has to do with Sanica and Biljani. In all the other places where Marko Adamovic appears as a name, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we know what was originally stated in the adjudicated facts but you are making this correction, then? You're saying that the person was not Adamovic, it was Samardzija?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't manage to this find this in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 18, that is where you mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, this paragraph is not in this text. Now I've looked at it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, what's written in your paragraph 18?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: "Adjudicated fact 2438 has been explained to me and this fact states, 'The commander of the Serb unit, Marko Adamovic, ordered the soldiers through a megaphone to set the village on fire and to kill the women and children.'" I can state the following: I categorically claim" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Then how about paragraph 9? And also Adamovic appears in para 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 9, no. In paragraph 3, paragraph 3 does not mention any names at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But paragraph 2 is correct. That's what you testified.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 is correct. And it stands, as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, I believe the witness may be referring to a paragraph about Mr. Samardzija that was taken out of the revised statement, so perhaps the easiest thing is simply to get him to confirm the two paragraphs in which Mr. Adamovic is referenced, just to clarify the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the paragraphs you looked at are all correct at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All the paragraphs I looked at are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it those mistakes pointed out by you must have been corrected. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Taking into account what you said about these paragraphs, does this statement as a whole now faithfully reflect what you have stated to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you today the same questions here in the courtroom, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would answer the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement into it evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number D4169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a short summary of Mr. Rajko Kalabic's statement in English. [In English] Rajko Kalabic was elected as the SDS deputy of the Council of Municipalities of the BiH Assembly to represent Kljuc municipality. He was also a member of the Kljuc Crisis Staff. The elections in the municipality of Kljuc were largely won by the SDS and SDA. Despite the fact that the SDS won over 50 per cent of the vote, all executive positions in the local authorities were divided equally between Muslim and Serbian personnel. At the time, there were no interethnic frictions in Kljuc, and Serbs and Muslims lived and worked together. The first incident in the territory of the Kljuc municipality happened on 27th of May, 1992, when an attack was mounted on a convoy of buses carrying demobilised JNA soldiers. During the attack, five soldiers were killed and one of the drivers was hanged from a tree by the road side, and his body hanged for several days until it was taken down by members of the VRS. Omer Filipovic, the Bosnian Muslim vice-president of the Municipal Assembly was in charge of the attack and the chairman of the Executive Committee of the Kljuc municipality, Asim Egrlic took also part in it and was wounded when the JNA convoy escorted -- escort returned fire. Nevertheless, he was administered first aid at the health centre in Kljuc and then he was transferred for further medical treatment in Banja Luka. These events caused fear and unrest among the residents of Kljuc. After that, a number of non-Serbs failed to turn up to -- for work because they were aware of the preparations being put in place by their leaders. All peace-loving non-Serbian residents of Kljuc who wanted to stay were allowed to keep their jobs and they regularly received their salaries. Anyone who expressed the wish to leave and was not suspected of having committed a criminal offence or a misdemeanour against the residents of Kljuc was allowed and enabled to leave. Regardless of the ethnicity, everyone who had somewhere to go and leave the pandemonium of war tried to leave. When leaving the municipality, all residents were allowed to sell their properties or to leave them to their fellow residents to look after. There was no plan for systematic destruction or plunder of these houses because each house was needed to accommodate refugees who were expelled from other towns of BH, where Muslims held power. Such acts of destructions were the work of extremist individuals and were met with condemnation by the population and the authorities at large. After the bloody events on 27th of May, 1992, the VRS units set up check-points on the access points to the town of Kljuc and tried to establish communication with the Muslim paramilitary commander Omer Filipovic. He was nearly begged not to proceed with his plan and to start negotiating instead. On 27th of May, 1992, the VRS unit collected weapons in those villages where Mr. Filipovic had his paramilitary units. Those Muslim militants who turned a deaf ear to the call to surrender weapons were brought in for criminal proceedings. The Serbian people believed in the state of Yugoslavia and therefore in the JNA as the army of its country, and for that reason they did not feel that they had to organise or arm. If weapons were procured, this was done by the individuals and this was therefore not directed by the SDS as the movement of the Serbian people in BH. On the other hand, the -- two other people in BH, Muslims and Croats, did not perceive the above-mentioned country and army as their own so they organised an armed paramilitary on the ground. At the time the role of the Crisis Staff involved only the methods of supplying people with food, water, and electricity. In addition the Crisis Staff also looked after the setting in motion of the commercial manufacture. During the war, the municipal organisation of the SDS in Kljuc did not meet and the claims that the SDS had devised and then implemented some plans against the non-Serbian population are therefore untrue. Dr. Karadzic did not have any influence on the elections of the officials or bodies in the municipality, either before the war or during the war. Dr. Karadzic never ordered, committed or aided and abetted war crimes against non-Serbian population in BH during the civil war. And that is short summary. At that moment I do not have additional questions for Mr. Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, as you have noted, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement, in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, as you state in your -- you note in your statement that you testified in the Brdjanin case here at the ICTY. That was in 2003; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Correct. I testified in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you also note that you testified in the case against Marko Adamovic and Bosko Lukic at the Bosnian state court, and that was -- you testified twice, once in the Defence of Mr. Lukic and once in the Defence of Mr. Adamovic, both times in 2010; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I testified in both cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you told the truth in your previous testimony before this Tribunal and the Bosnian state court?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I told the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like at the outset to clarify the various positions that you held because it's not entirely clear from your statement. You say that you were an SDS deputy in the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in paragraph 3 of your statement. You were also a member of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you were subsequently a member of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, as you state in your statement. You were also a member of the Crisis Staff which was formed on the 23rd of December, 1991, in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you were subsequently a member of the War Presidency which was formed on the 10th of July in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 5 of your statement, you're discussing the period between the multi-party elections and the 27th of May, 1992. You state that at that time there were no interethnic frictions in Kljuc. It's true, though, isn't it, that in the summer of 1991, the Kljuc SDS began to organise memorial services for the Serb victims of World War II. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. At some point, memorial services were held for the victims of World War II who were buried near Kljuc, and that place is still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to talk about one of these memorial services which was held on the 29th of September, 1991, was organised by the SDS jointly celebrating its anniversary and -- or the establishment of the Kljuc SDS and commemorating the victims of the Ustasha genocide. Now, you spoke at that event; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we have P3423, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This, Mr. Kalabic, is a record of that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And towards the bottom of the page in the English, we will see what you said at that assembly. And you noted that: This was the first occasion after World War II when we were actually reminded of the genocide which the Ustashas committed against the Serbian people, rather late but still in time to prevent history from repeating itself in its most horrible form. A foul war was being waged in one part of the country, typified by the unleashing of a genocidal fascist hysteria on the part of the hordes controlled by and serving the goal of the pro-fascist and pro-Ustasha newly elected Croatian government? Now, do you agree, Mr. Kalabic, that this kind of public speech would have raised interethnic tensions in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I cannot read this in this document. Maybe you can show it to me so I remember that I really said these things and then perhaps I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's towards the bottom of the document, I believe. And just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this a record of that event or the broadcast of certain radio?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's a journalistic reporting of the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a reporting of a journalist on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If you would like me to refresh your memory, you confirmed in your Brdjanin testimony that this was what you said at that event.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, since I don't have the text of my speech, I cannot remember exactly what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can collapse the English for the moment. Yes, we can zoom in the last paragraph. I think I see your name here, if you could read that out. You can read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. I am not really sure that I used these words quoted here in my speech, but I don't think that at that time my speech was disruptive to the interethnic relations in Kljuc because, at that time, it is true that those symbols that had been used in 1941 and in the Second World War had reappeared in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in our eyes, they were seen as a threat to our lives, to peace, et cetera, and we had to sound a warning against such things. At that time, however, we did not yet know that these symbols would be adopted as the official emblems of the new Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I'd like to remind you what you said when you accepted that you said these words in your Brdjanin testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And that's -- could we please have 25682, and it's e-court page 11. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This is the record of your testimony in the Brdjanin case, Mr. Kalabic, and the quote from that rally was put to you and you were asked at the bottom of the page: "What are you talking about there?" And then you go on to explain exactly what you were talking about and you explain, as you just did, that this was the first opportunity for the newly elected multi-party - if we could move to the next page, please - government and you explained what you were talking about? And then you were asked: "When you say 'what's happening again,' what do you mean?" And you say: "What I meant at that time," and you continue to explain what you meant at that time. So it's clear, isn't it, Mr. Kalabic, that you did, in fact, say these things?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to see these pages in the Serbian language so that I can see what's written there and then I could comment. I asked for the same thing a moment ago but instead I got some writing by a journalist instead of the text of my speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender these two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you read out the relevant part of the transcript, from the bottom of previous page?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, as I said, the passage that I just read out was put to you and you were asked: "What are you talking about there?" And you say: "This was the first opportunity for the newly elected multiparty government after the socialist times in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina to speak more realistically of what happened in 1941, who the victims were, who the perpetrators were, and what is happening again. And are these -- are the things that are happening again something that would remind us of the things that happened before in 1941?" So do you accept that in that passage, you're commenting on the words that you used in the speech?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, may I just ask one thing? Why is it mentioned at all that it would be addressed to the assembly? It's on the previous page. It was not an assembly meeting. It was a rally connected with a funeral. And the words on the previous page referred to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether assembly was referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we put on the previous page again, we'll see it. Line 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This, Mr. Karadzic, this is a quote from the document and the document identifies itself as a record of the SDS event which jointly celebrates the SDS Kljuc anniversary and the -- and commemorates the victims of the Ustasha genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So it's clear, isn't it, Mr. Kalabic, that in your Brdjanin testimony you accepted that you said those words?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Well, without a translation, I cannot say quite decidedly what I meant and what I said. But taken out of context, these two passages could be interpreted to have a totally different connotation. However, the truth is that those symbols reemerging at that time did take one's mind back to 1941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive those two transcript pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6550, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, other events that were happening around that time were the proclamation by the Assembly of the Bosanska Krajina, of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, on the 16th of September, 1991, for the parties' reference that's P3421; the circulation by Mr. Brdjanin of an SDS order from a meeting of the ARK municipal presidents chaired by Mr. Karadzic, and that's P3581; and there is evidence before the Trial Chamber, Mr. Kalabic, that both of these had a negative impact on interethnic relations, specifically with the Bosnian Muslim community, resulting in the SDA and the MBO making joint public statements about that negative impact, and for the parties' reference that's P3577 and P3582. Is it your evidence that you, as an assembly member for Kljuc and a member of the ARK Assembly, you were unaware of the negative impact that these moves by the Serbs' authorities were having on interethnic relations?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would need to see the document and then I would be able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I don't think you do need to see the document. Do you recall the proclamation of the ARK in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the proclamation of the ARK in September 1991. That's why I said I would need to see a document. That would refresh my memory of things I used to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break? We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I'm going to move on to a different topic. In paragraph 16 of your statement, you say that Dr. Karadzic did not have any influence on the election of the officials or bodies in the municipality either before the war or after the war. But it's true, isn't it, that the Kljuc Crisis Staff was formed pursuant to the instructions on the organisation and activities of the Serbian people which was issued by Mr. Karadzic? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic did not personally say who would be on the Crisis Staff. He did not give the name and surname of a person who would be on the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, you were present at the 20th of December, 1991, meeting at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo at which Mr. Karadzic distributed the instructions that we've just mentioned, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether I was at that meeting at the Holiday Inn or not, so I cannot remember at all, I cannot remember having that document in my hands.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I ask where is the reference for the assertion that I have been distributing that? I was not a technical person there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that could be understood in the context by the witness. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have page 74 of 65 ter 25682, Mr. Kalabic's testimony in Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to focus at the bottom of this page, please. You were asked. "... you saw a copy of the instructions for the organisation of the Serbian people in Sarajevo." And you said: "Yes, I did say that I saw this instruction in Sarajevo." So it's correct, isn't it, Mr. Kalabic, that you saw the instructions in Sarajevo at the Holiday Inn meeting?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember. I cannot remember being at this meeting at the Holiday Inn at all, and I particularly cannot remember seeing this kind of document. Is it possible for me to receive a copy of this document in my language to take a look at it? Then that would be, I mean, reasonable. Then I could say what I have to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, we will shortly look at a document in your language dealing exactly with this subject, but it's your testimony that you remember nothing about this meeting. You don't remember, as you testified in Brdjanin, that the instructions were given to SDS representatives who brought the instructions to their respective municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I do not remember being at that meeting at all. And, in particular, I do not remember that I took some document and took it to the Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender pages 74 and 75, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you show us page 75 or read out --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, on page 75, the witness stated the document wasn't given to representatives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you'd like to tender that, put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Sorry, I paraphrased it. I'll read the exact passage to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, you stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kalabic, you stated, with respect to these instructions, you were asked: Was it given to representatives in the assembly to take back to their own municipalities? And you responded: No, it wasn't given to representatives in the assembly; it was given to representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party, and they were the ones who brought these instructions to their respective municipalities."

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, so what is it that I've already said, that I did not see the document, that it was not given to me in Sarajevo, that I do not remember it and now the Prosecutor confirmed all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, the Tribunal does not make a transcript in B/C/S. It's only in working language of the Tribunal, both in English and French. But audio tape is kept. If you'd like you can check whether you said -- testified like this or not. I think you know this already. We will add these two pages to the exhibit which is Exhibit P6550. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have P2592?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, this, Mr. Kalabic, is a document in your own language and it's dated the 23rd of December, 1991, and it's the minutes of a meeting of the Executive Committee of the SDS Municipal Board in Kljuc. And you'll see that agenda item 1 of this meeting is: Briefing on the decisions of the Serbian Assembly and the materials that arrived. And if you look at the discussion of item 1, it states: "Veljko Kondic informed the meeting of the instructions for the organisation and activities of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. All organs will be required to act in accordance with the instructions."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Before -- could we just please go to page 2 of this meeting. In both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And it states: "After a recess, Rajko Kalabic informed those present on the issues considered in the second part of the Serbian Assembly proceedings." So, Mr. Kalabic, this meeting of the Kljuc authorities took place three days after the meeting in Sarajevo, and it's you and Veljko Kondic informing the Kljuc SDS of Mr. Karadzic's instructions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: This document does not show what it is that I was making the assembly aware of, or, rather, I mean, the Executive Board of the SDS. However, I mean, when I would return from sessions of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska, I would briefly provide information about certain topics that were discussed at the assembly and that went on for years, for as long as this assembly worked. This just shows that Rajko Kalabic informed about the other part of the assembly, it doesn't say exactly what it was. Now, what is contained in this other part, that is something I don't know right now and I cannot remember what it was that I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We've just seen -- let's look at what you and Mr. Kondic were talking about. You've just seen the passage where Mr. Kondic informed the meeting of the instructions and stated that all organs will be required to act in accordance with the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And if we could go back to that passage on pages 1 of the English and B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have seen it. So collapse the English and zoom in in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm going to refer to a slightly different passage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And after Mr. Kondic informs the members, Brane Vojvodic says: "I can accept all Karadzic's proposals without seeing them." And Mr. Kondic says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's on page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My apologies. Perhaps it's on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So Mr. Vojvodic says he can accept all of Karadzic's proposals without seeing them. Mr. Kondic says: "That means that all suggestions and tasks from the instructions are accepted in their entirety." And he then proposes or proceeds to detail the composition of the Kljuc Crisis Staff. So it's clear from this document, isn't it, that the Kljuc Crisis Staff was formed directly pursuant to Mr. Karadzic's instructions?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was formed at the proposal of Veljko Kondic, the way he saw the instructions and how he found out about them and how he --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kalabic, could you please repeat the end of the sentence more clearly as the interpreters did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was formed as dictated by Mr. Veljko Kondic, in the sense in which he understood the instructions on the basis of which he dictated this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You've stated that you can't recall what you said at this meeting, so let's look at what you said. As we noted, you informed those present on the issues considered in the second part of the Serbian Assembly proceedings. And if we look at Milan Jovicic's statement, he says: "I ask that this meeting be informed about the second stage." And you respond: "The first stage is the preparation for the second stage, so there is no need to introduce the second stage." Now, this, Mr. Kalabic, is a reference to the second stage of the instructions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I commented on Milan Jovicic's position because I personally thought at that moment, since Veljko Kondic did say a few sentences in relation to instructions A, and his sentences had to do with the establishment of a Crisis Staff, my position was that it was not necessary for us to be made aware of anything else because in the municipality of Kljuc, plan A or plan B was not needed because the president of the municipality was from the SDS, that is to say a member of the Serb people, then also a majority in the assembly, and quite a few people in the executive government. It wasn't even necessary to establish a Crisis Staff, let alone move towards certain instructions of a different kind because we felt no need to have that done. And realistically speaking, there wasn't a need for that. And that's why that is what I said during the discussion, that there was no need for us to read anything further or interpret anything because, in fact, I mean, we did have a majority in the municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I'm not sure that you've answered my question. My question is: Is your reference in these minutes, that is a reference to the second stage of the instructions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Well, give me that page. Let me take a look at it, because it's not in front of me now. Let me see now what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to look at page 22 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Are we on the correct page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The relevant passage that we are interested in is: "The first stage is preparation for the second stage, so there is no need to introduce the second stage."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Kalabic? Yes, I think it's here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So having seen it, can you confirm --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it had to do with that, precisely, that it was not necessary to familiarise oneself with any other document because Veljko Kondic had already presented what was necessary from the first document, and presented how a Crisis Staff is to be established. Since the SDS already had a majority in the authorities in the municipality, there was no need to do anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I have to say it is the translation that causes a great deal of confusion. The witness interpreted this correctly now: It was not necessary to familiarise oneself with, et cetera. Whereas over here in the English translation, it says: "Introduction."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So if I understand your testimony, you're saying that, yes, this is a reference to the second stage of the instructions, but at that stage, you were not -- it was not necessary to familiarise yourself with that second stage?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was no need for the municipal board of the SDS to be made aware of the second stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's come on to the second stage of the instructions now. You were present on the 14th of February, 1992, at the Holiday Inn meeting in Sarajevo where Mr. Karadzic told the members of the SDS that the second stage of the instructions should be implemented. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember, first of all, that I was present at all; and secondly, I do not remember. I mean, if I was not present, then I cannot remember that this kind of sentence was uttered. On the other hand, as far as Kljuc is concerned, again, I repeat, the second stage, no one in Kljuc was made aware of that and did not become familiar with it. That includes me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 5721?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This, Mr. Kalabic, is a receipt from the Holiday Inn hotel --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we have pages -- page 6 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So this is a receipt from the Holiday Inn hotel for SDS Assembly members and you'll see that it's dated 14th of February, arrival; departure, 15th of February. So this shows that you were, in fact, at that meeting, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this bill practically doesn't show a thing. First of all, it says down here "signature of guest" and there is no signature of mine there. That is one thing. Secondly, whenever I went to Sarajevo, I would only stay at a private apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6551, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Simply that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you told the Court that you have no idea what was said at that meeting so I'd just like to remind you of what was said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And could we please have P12? If I could have page 5 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, please? And the passage I'm interested in is at the very bottom of the English and in the middle of the page of the B/C/S. This is Mr. Karadzic speaking. And he says: "That is" -- I think we need to move slightly further down in the English, please. "That is, if you remember, who keeps that in mind or maybe not on his person a stage number 2. There is, remember," if we can move to the next page, "you know what I'm talking about, we know. Yes, that is therefore the stage number 2, the second stage in smaller or bigger variations, but you have to implement that slowly now." If we could move to page 24 of the English and page 18 of the B/C/S, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: At the top of the page in the B/C/S, Mr. Kalabic, and just before it says "cut in recording," Mr. Karadzic says: "That is why we called you here today, to intensify, to introduce the second level, and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory." Now, Mr. Kalabic, four days later, you reported back to the SDS municipal board in Kljuc on that meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I please be shown the beginning of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says quite clearly that it is the expanded session of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party held on the 14th of February, 1992, in Sarajevo at the Holiday Inn hotel. I was not a member of the Main Board or the Executive Board of the SDS, and so I can quite rightly claim that I did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we move into closed session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Private, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Private session, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No worry, we use it interchangeably. I will make sure when closed session is required.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, not just before the conflict but during the conflict, bodies were set up pursuant to Karadzic's instructions, and specifically, this Trial Chamber has received evidence that the Kljuc War Presidency, of which you were a member, was set up pursuant to Karadzic's decision; and the references for that are P2643, P3454 and P2369. So it's not at all true, is it, Mr. Kalabic, that Mr. Karadzic had no influence on the bodies in the municipality before or during the war? In fact, before the war, the Crisis Staff was set up on his instructions, the second level of the instructions were activated when he said it was time to do so, and during the war, the War Presidency was established pursuant to his order. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I can't say that that is the truth because there was almost no contact with Mr. Karadzic unless one went to the assembly from time to time. For a certain period of time it was not possible to reach Pale because there was fighting all around, so it was impossible to get through. And the telephone lines were down, there was no electricity either, there were even problems in providing the inhabitants with general provisions, food, sugar, flour, bread, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I think you're straying off the topic. We are talking about bodies being introduced or established pursuant to Mr. Karadzic's order or instructions. And if I understand your testimony, despite the documents that we've seen today, it's your position that none of those bodies were established pursuant to Mr. Karadzic's order or instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. Could the reference please be provided to this witness's testimony? Was he talking about personal decisions or about institutions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the point of your objections. Overruled. Shall we continue? You can take up the issue in your re-examination, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I don't believe you answered my question. My question is: Despite the documents that we have seen today, the evidence before this Trial Chamber, your position is that nothing happened pursuant to -- nothing was established pursuant to Mr. Karadzic's instructions or orders? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I said in my earlier testimony that given the report of Mr. -- there was a report from Mr. Veljko Kondic which had to do with the establishment of the Crisis Staff and pursuant to that report a Crisis Staff was established. I said that Mr. Karadzic did not have any personal influence on anything in relation to Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different topic. Now, in paragraph 7 of your statement, you say that nothing special was noticed until the 27th of May, 1992. But contrary to that contention, Mr. Kalabic, it's true, isn't it, that on the 7th of May, large numbers of military troops were transferred onto the territory of Kljuc in order to assist in the take-over and declaration of the Serbian Municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I have to say that on the 7th of May, power wasn't seized in Kljuc because the -- to a large extent, the SDS had power together with the SDA. We had our president of the municipality, we had a lot of people in the executive government and we had majority assembly. So there was no need to take over power in the assembly because the SDS was exercising power in Kljuc, it couldn't take power over from itself. So let me conclude, if I may, as far as I know, there were no troops, no significant numbers of troops that came to Kljuc. Although at that time, since there was a war in Croatia, various sorts of troops did pass through. I didn't pay much attention to that. And I do have to say that that date is important for one reason alone. And that is that on the basis of the laws in force in Republika Srpska, as Yugoslavia no longer existed, there was the flag of Yugoslavia on the municipality building. And at that time, a decision was taken to take that flag down because that state no longer existed and the decision was taken to raise the flag of Republika Srpska because the Serbs were in the majority there. So that decision was taken. Similarly, the symbols, the signs, on people in uniform were changed on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was: Were there significant troops involved in the Kljuc area and it had to do with taking over power in Kljuc. That was the essence of the question, and I think that I have mostly answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your answer, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is that there was no significant army presence in Kljuc municipality. Power wasn't seized in the municipality of Kljuc because the Serbs were in power in Kljuc. They were in the majority, they had their president of the municipality and they had a majority in the assembly, so there was no need for them to take over power. And thirdly --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I believe that's the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P3663.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your answer is there was no take-over of power in Kljuc and there was no significant number of troops on the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to see page 5 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
