utterances.text: And Mr. Kalabic, while we are waiting for those pages, I'd like to explain that this is a military report regarding the activities of the 6th Brigade in the period relevant to our discussions. And at the very top of the page in the B/C/S, you'll see that it states that from the 7th of May, 1992, to 10th of May, 1992, together with units from Kljuc, a part of the 6th Brigade units, i.e. parts of the 1st and 3rd Battalions, the Crni Djordje Intervention Platoon, a police platoon, and a reconnaissance platoon participated in taking over power in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I have heard something of this kind. This is the first time heard about the Crni Djordje Platoon, and I can claim with -- I can claim that there was no such thing in Kljuc. I don't know if there was anyone around Kljuc, in the vicinity, but there was no one in Kljuc and there was no take-over, that's for sure. The president of the municipality was in his office. The flag was replaced, in front of the window of his office, the Yugoslav flag was taken down and the Republika Srpska flag was raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's look at the announcement of the Kljuc Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, could we see further references, further details? Who signed this document? Who issued the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I can also refer Mr. Karadzic on this topic to P3586 on the topic of the take-over and the 6th Brigade in Kljuc and the take-over and declaration of the Serbian Municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I'd like to show you a document, the announcement from the Kljuc Crisis Staff, that is your Crisis Staff, on the 7th of May, and that's P3497.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting for that, your Excellency, I'm surprised, I don't know where this document comes from because there is nothing that would justify its description as a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We discussed it already and then it was admitted into evidence. You can raise it in your closing argument, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So you'll see, Mr. Kalabic, this is a public announcement from the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Kljuc and it's dated the 8th of May because it states in the first line: "The Crisis Staff of the municipality of Kljuc hereby informs all citizens that yesterday, on the 7th of May, certain changes were made in the Kljuc Public Security Station." What I'm interested in is at page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. And the third-to-last paragraph states: "Citizens are informed that the increased presence of armed forces on the territory of the municipality should not be understood as an attack on the freedom of -- or safety of any nation." So here, we see the Crisis Staff, of which you were a member, telling people not to be alarmed because of the increased presence of armed forces on the territory and yet you claim to be totally unaware of the significant number of troops.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I really wasn't aware of the fact that there was an increased presence of troops there, and this really wasn't noticeable in Kljuc, that this announcement here was made as it was made, and that was the situation. It has to do with the fact that only the flag was changed and the signs or symbols that men in uniform were wearing were also changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, at paragraph 14 of your statement, you state that during the war the municipal organisations of the SDS in Kljuc did not meet. But do you agree, as is the evidence before this Trial Chamber, that first the Crisis Staff and then subsequently the War Presidency met regularly throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff did meet during this period, especially after the 27th of May, five, six or 10 days later. But the municipal board of the SDS wasn't functioning because there was a ban on the functioning of the Serbian Democratic Party at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: At paragraph 9 of your statement, you describe how Colonel Galic informed the Crisis Staff that he had appointed Marko Adamovic commander of the town defence. And you go on to say that the Crisis Staff involved only -- was involved only in the matters of supplying people with food, water and electricity rather than military matters. On this topic, I'd like to show you P2643. This, as you see, Mr. Kalabic, is a report of 29th July of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff War Presidency -- sorry, on the work of the Crisis Staff War Presidency of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly in the period from 15th of May, 1992, to the present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 of both the English and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to focus on the paragraph beginning, "Throughout the armed conflict ..." And it states: "Throughout the armed conflict, representatives, commanders, of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regularly participated in the sessions of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency. These representatives were in command of and conducted combat activities to defend the territory and citizens of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly against Muslim extremists, and maintained good cooperation and coordination with the Crisis Staff of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly. All major questions related to the army and police were resolved within the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly. This period can be described as one of very successful cooperation between the Crisis Staff and the military organs in crushing the armed resistance by Muslim extremists." So now, this is a more accurate account of the relationship between the civilian and the military authorities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: At that time, the Crisis Staff was standing in for the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc because most of the deputies were indeed in the units of the VRS all along the front lines. So it was very difficult for them to convene or attend meetings. So the Crisis Staff was doing the job of the assembly. And generally speaking, the Crisis Staff was made up of people who were officials in the executive authorities, and they did their jobs, their executive functions, in their own departments. The army, on the other hand, had its own hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, let me clarify my question. Do you agree, as you did in your Brdjanin testimony, that there was cooperation, good cooperation, between the civilian and military authorities at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The cooperation between the Crisis Staff and the army existed only in certain aspects, such as procurement of the members of the servicemen's families, supplying food, ensuring that children can go to school, that they have enough to buy flour. The Crisis Staff did exclusively that sort of thing. And the army did its job, and functioned along its own chain of command and hierarchy, to which they adhered very strictly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see P2606? I'd like page 3 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The document we are about to look at is a book of minutes from sessions of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff, and I'd like to focus your attention on a passage from the 27th of May, 1992. And it's number 10, point number 10 in this document. It's at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, and it states: "The relationship between the military and civilian authorities will be as follows: The military authorities will follow the orders of the civilian authorities. The civilian authorities will not interfere with the way they are followed." So, Mr. Kalabic, that's the truth, isn't it? This was how the cooperation worked in practice?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Maybe somebody wrote that but in practice it didn't work like that. In practice, it worked completely differently. The Crisis Staff did its own work and the army functioned along its own hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You and other members of the Crisis Staff wore military uniforms and carried weapons; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak into the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After doing my military service, as a young man, I became a member of the reserve police instead a member of the Territorial Defence, and as such I was issued with a weapon and a uniform. As a member of the Crisis Staff, I put on my uniform when I went to tour units on the front lines, on the territory of the municipality of Kljuc. I didn't wear it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: All members of the Kljuc Crisis Staff and War Presidency wore uniforms, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: No. Slobodan Jurisic never put on a uniform. Veljko Kondic either. The president of the municipality wore a uniform because he was a huge man, weighing over 150 kilos, and the uniform was more comfortable for him than a jacket.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 25682, and I'd like to see page 140.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And at line 15 of this testimony, your testimony in the Brdjanin case, Mr. Kalabic, you say: "For a time, at the very beginning, all the members of the War Presidency, that is, the Crisis Staff, wore uniforms, and so did I." And were you asked: "Why?" And your response is: "That was the decision, and I abided by it for the most part." So that's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: That was indeed the decision, but it was not binding. And in the first two days, the 27th and 28th, that indeed happened, but it didn't apply to the majority of the people. I wore that uniform the first two days, and after that only when I went to tour units. Slobodan Jurisic, who was a member of the Crisis Staff, never put on a uniform. Veljko Kondic, the president of the SDS board, never put on a uniform. Dr. Dragan Smiljanic, member of the Crisis Staff, never put on a uniform. And that's -- that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, Mr. Kalabic, that as a member of the War Presidency, on the basis of a decision allowing you to move around in uniform and carry weapons, you carried weapons; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I carried a weapon only when I went to tour military units, and even then not every time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender these two pages, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, once again, I have not -- I read the passage from the second question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will add this page 140 [Realtime transcript read in error "P142"] to Exhibit P6550.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, it's also in evidence before the Trial Chamber that the Crisis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said page 140, e-court page 140. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's also in evidence before this Trial Chamber that the Crisis Staff and subsequently the War Presidency were involved in establishing and equipping the 17th Light Infantry Brigade of the VRS. And the references for that are P2643, P3455 and P3452. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My question is: It's correct that the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency were involved in establishing and equipping the 17th Light Infantry Brigade of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question because I don't understand with what the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency could equip a military unit. A military unit needs uniforms, weapons, rolling stock, assets, all the things the Crisis Staff did not have. I don't understand the question, so I can't answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The evidence of the type of -- the evidence of that equipment is before the Trial Chamber, but I will move on. I'd like to focus on one of the meetings between the civilian and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P3590?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, this is a meeting dated 14th of July, 1992, with presidents of municipalities, and it is -- you'll see at page 1 that present at the meeting are the commander of the 30th Partizan Division, Colonel Galic; the commander of the 6th Partizan Brigade, Colonel Basara; at number 4, the commander of the Kljuc TO, Bosko Lukic; at 5, the president of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly, Jovo Banjac; and at number 11, you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 2 of the English and 2 of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This is Colonel Galic briefing the participants on the AOR of the 30th Partizan Division and he states, in respect of Kljuc, after the partial take-over of power, the situation in the territory of Kljuc municipality is relatively calm. And he then goes on to describe the various different units that were securing Kljuc at the time of the take-over of power. Now, the 9th Corps, the 5th Corps, these were the troops that you earlier said you were unaware of; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I don't know about these forces. I don't know what they were doing. And as for the 5th Corps, and the Light Brigade, I know they existed. I know certain brigades existed such as the 30th Brigade near Mrkonjic, but I cannot specifically now maintain that this one was in a certain place or wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's move to page 3 of this document, please, in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And here, the document describes how the president of Mrkonjic Grad Municipal Assembly presented the conclusions from the meeting held in Banja Luka. And it states -- if you look in the next passage, it states: The strategic goals formulated at the meeting in Banja Luka were presented, and it goes on to list six strategic goals. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And then could we please move to page 4 of the English and 4 of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And at the top of the page in the English, we see that the -- these are the conclusions that were proposed by Colonel Galic, and he states: Implement the decisions from the meeting in Banja Luka but submit them to the commands of units and municipalities. So this is how the cooperation between the military and the civilian organs in Kljuc happened in reality. The strategic goals that were disseminated at the meeting in Banja Luka were then implemented by the army and the municipality commands; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Municipalities did not have commands. They had their own president, not commander. There was no such thing as commander of the municipality. The civilian authorities cooperated with the army to the extent I described. The Crisis Staff, that is to say the municipality, helped the army by procuring food, footwear and clothing, to the extent they were able to afford it. There was no other cooperation between the Crisis Staff of the municipality and the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, that's not at all true, on the basis of this document. This document shows that the civilian authorities were heavily involved in coordinating and assisting the military in their shared goals.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Not in terms of coordinating and assisting the military, but, yes, the civilian authorities did receive some information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, you attended the 16th session of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly meeting on the 12th of May in Banja Luka, didn't you? The 12th of May meeting that is the subject of this report.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was present at the session in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And then on the 14th of May, you briefed your colleagues in Kljuc on the decisions and the reports from that session; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I can't remember but I suppose I briefed the people from the municipality with the conclusions of that assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's -- let's refresh our memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P3439. You'll see these are minutes of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff from the 13th and 14th of May. If we could go to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus on -- your attention on item 2, which states: Jovo Banjac, president of the Crisis Staff, and Rajko Kalabic, deputy of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly, advised the members of the Crisis Staff of the positions and the security situation in Kljuc municipality in connection with the decisions and reports from a session of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly. And then just below that we see the conclusion, the report in connection with the decisions and reports from a session of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly is adopted. So that's what happened, isn't it? You went to the meeting, you came back from the 12th of May Banja Luka meeting, you briefed your colleagues on what had happened on that meeting, and you and your colleagues adopted the decisions and reports from that assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I certainly briefed the people from the municipality with the conclusions of the assembly, and I can't remember these decisions as stated here, but probably there were conclusions involved at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I'd like to move on to a totally different topic. At paragraph 23 of your statement, regarding adjudicated fact 2438, which is -- which deals with Mr. Marko Adamovic ordering soldiers, through a megaphone, in Prhovo, on the 1st of June, to set the village on fire and kill women and children, you state that Marko Adamovic visited the offices of the municipality on several occasions that day and could not have been in several places. And you also state that, to your knowledge, Mr. Adamovic was acquitted of any responsibility for that. Now, yesterday, the Chamber heard from Mr. Adamovic that, in fact, he's currently awaiting the verdict in his retrial, but I'd like to focus on your previous testimony on this issue. Now, in Mr. Adamovic's trial, the first time you testified on this issue as a Defence witness for Bosko Lukic, you stated that you remembered the incident of Prhovo very well because you were coming and going from the office of Crisis Staff President Jovo Banjac, the commander of the military police came in crying and said that a military police officer had gotten killed, things had gotten out of control and women and children had been killed. That's correct, isn't it? That was your testimony.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I don't understand whether Jovo Banjac was going from one office to another, coming and going. But as I said before, sometime in the afternoon, an active duty officer came into Jovo's office, addressed Galic and told him through tears that he had lost one military policeman at Prhovo, and after that, he lost control over the military police, which led to that incident in which a number of women, children and elderly people got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The second time --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Must be some confusion with numbers. Paragraph 23 does not contain this what is said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic, for that clarification. I'm referring to paragraph 18 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the second time you testified on this issue, before the state court in Bosnia as a Defence witness for Mr. Adamovic, you provided the additional detail that he was also present when the military commander came in crying with this news. Is this the account of events that you stand by today?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must say that I'm getting the impression that some things are being conflated here, and with your leave, I would like to say exactly what I had stated. First of all, concerning my testimony regarding Bosko Lukic, as far as I'm able to recall today, I don't think Marko Adamovic was named in the Prosecutor's question so I didn't need to talk about him at that time. And concerning Marko Adamovic, he was mentioned as a possible, potential commander of the army in that area, and I only said the things that are true. I know that on the 1st of June, 1992, on several occasions, he went into the office of the president, Jovo Banjac, carrying a little agenda in his hand that he always had, and in the afternoon, one active duty officer came into Jovo Banjac's office - I can't remember if he was a captain first class or just captain - turned to Colonel Galic and said, through tears, that he had lost one military policeman and then he simply lost control as a commander over the military police. And the military police then created that incident in which a number of women, children and elderly people were killed. That was my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banjac -- or Mr. Kalabic, rather, I would like to show you the account that you gave in the Brdjanin case in relation to this incident seven years previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And that is -- could we please have P -- 65 ter 25682, page 151.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You were asked: "Were you aware that on the 1st of June, the village of Prhovo was attacked?" And you respond: "I received that information later on. Not I, but we were informed at the Crisis Staff about Prhovo." You were asked: Were you also told that the men who had been taken from the village were separated from the women and lined up along the road towards Peci?" You said: "At the Crisis Staff we did not receive such detailed information." And you were asked: "Well, did you receive information that some civilians, people without arms, people under guard, were killed on that road?" And you responded: The information about casualties in that area we received later on. But this information was not thorough. We didn't have the full detail." And you were asked specifically: "Were you aware that women and children were killed during the attack on Prhovo?" And you say: "I said that we received that information later on." If we could just turn to the next page, and it's still in the context of the discussion of these events, and you say at line 13 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. It's not about these events. It's about Velagici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic is asked: "When you received this information, before we come to the Velagici killings," and then they continue to discuss this incident. So continuing to discuss this incident, you state: "It was only after the event that the information reached us. Whether this was on the same day or one or two days after the events, I can't say." So now, Mr. Kalabic, in contrast to your testimony at the Adamovic trial in 2010, where you remembered very specific details and your testimony today, in fact, where you remember extremely specific details as to when and how you and Mr. Adamovic heard about the Prhovo killings, in your testimony in 2003, you stated that you received information that women and children were killed in Prhovo sometime after the events, and whether it was on the same day or one or two days after the events, you couldn't say. And your later account, your account that you gave in the Adamovic trial and the account that you're giving this Trial Chamber today, it's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 1st of June, 1992, I found out at the president's office from an active duty officer who addressed Mr. Galic, I found out what I already spoke about. As for additional information, additional information, I mean, well, I did not have a lot of this information that is being treated here today before this Court. Of course, a day or two or three or -- days later, yes, of course, but that's the real truth. However, in the Brdjanin case, and in my answers to the questions, no one was mentioned personally, so I could not have mentioned the name and surname of a particular person who was being mentioned here today because I had no idea that he was nearby. And I know where he was at that point in time and I said that today before this Court, and I stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender pages 151 and 152.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. These will be added to the exhibit. Do you have further examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that I'm at the end of my time but I would ask the Court's indulgence for some further time to use with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much further? How much more time are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd appreciate 30 minutes, but I'm in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will take a break, after which I would like you to try to finish in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is minded to take a break for an hour. Would there be any problem with the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I appreciate it. We will resume at 1.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, at statement -- at paragraph 34 of your statement, you say that the treatment of Muslim civilians in a combat zone was in accordance with the law and you cite the example of Velagici. I'd like to talk about the incident that happened in Velagici on the 1st of June, the same date as the incident in Prhovo that we've just been discussing. And there is evidence before this Trial Chamber that men from the local villages were instructed by the Serb authorities to come to Velagici for certificates of freedom of movement to be issued to them, and so following this order, a column of these men walked to Velagici holding a white flag and presented themselves at Velagici school, and none of these men who walked to Velagici were armed. For the parties' reference that's P713, transcript pages 9121 and 9125. Now, Mr. Kalabic, you heard of this incident on the day that it happened, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about what happened at the end. However, I did not fully understand that question, because in paragraph 34, I'm talking about certain things, Pudin Han, Velagici, Krasulje, and I talk about the population that was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let me -- your evidence in paragraph 34 -- your statement is in evidence. I'm asking you to focus on the events in Velagici on the 1st of June. Do you confirm that you heard of them on the day that they happened?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: As for my knowledge concerning Velagici, it belongs to the following, what I will say now. As for combat in Velagici, there were paramilitaries, Muslim paramilitary soldiers -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be allowed to say what he's got to say rather than put a complicated question and a twisted question seeking an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But when you asked "heard of them on the day," what are "they"? It was -- you read out or summarised all the evidence. So I'll allow the witness to continue. But please be brief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the operations on the 27th of May, 1992, I mean these things happened at Velagici, since it was known, I mean, that the Army of Republika Srpska would enter -- or, rather, invite the paramilitaries to hand over their weapons, via Radio Kljuc, the inhabitants of Pudin Han and Velagici were asked to seek shelter in the area of Kljuc so that there would not be any undesirable consequences. Most of the population, women, children, old men, people who did not belong to the civilian defence, they sought shelter there and they were protected there. After the operations at Pudin Han and Velagici ended, the population was taken back to their villages on buses. Now, my information as to what happened in Velagici itself is as follows. In the Office of the President of the municipality, there was General Galic and he asked the president of the municipality to send buses to Velagici so that those people who had been brought in would be picked up by two buses and transported to the area of the military barracks in Manjaca. The bus drivers went to that area and returned very quickly, upset, because they said that they did not find any living people there. They found people who had been killed. Colonel Galic was very upset. He swore. And that is the information I have. What else do I know? I know that people who were appointed by the military command to stand guard by that school where this happened, I know that these persons were arrested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I asked to you be brief. I think you answered the question. Please continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, you've explained about this meeting with Mr. Galic. Do you confirm that that happened -- I'm sorry. You've confirmed that on the day of these events, you were told that every one of the people who was held at Velagici had been killed. Do you also confirm that you knew -- or that those people were unarmed?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I don't know that they were armed. On the contrary, what was stated was that it was the members of the Territorial Defence who were armed. If somebody was unarmed, that means that they had thrown away their weapons when they surrendered or they had hidden them somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And the people who were detained at Velagici school, who, as you have testified, were all killed, those people were unarmed; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: These people were armed during the combat operations, and as prisoners they were unarmed. That is why this group that did that was prosecuted. They were not supposed to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Do you agree, as you did in your Brdjanin testimony, that this was the most appalling war crime?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Certainly, the killing of so many people can be considered a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And despite your claim today that the people, the group that did it was prosecuted, are you aware that after this appalling war crime, rather than insisting that the perpetrators be punished, the Kljuc authorities lobbied for charges against the perpetrators to be dropped? For the parties' reference that's P3616.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, wouldn't it be more accurate to name the person as opposed to the Kljuc authorities. It seemed like my recollection of that exhibit there was one particular individual. We don't know if he was acting on behalf of the authorities or in his personal capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Moving to the incident at Biljani school on the 10th of July. In paragraph 19 of your statement, you say that those who were rounded up were found in possession of illegal weapons or suspected to have weapons and were brought in to be processed, based on submissions that they were members of the paramilitary forces. Do you agree, Mr. Kalabic, that the killings at Biljani school were also massacres, killings, of unarmed people?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the previous question remained unanswered and it is very important. Would you allow me to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. She just moved on. Can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this question, I did not have any knowledge about what was happening there, so I mean, I cannot give any comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we have page 154 of 65 ter 25682?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And at line 13, you were discussing -- you were asked by the Prosecutor, who said: "... I'm talking about massacres, killings of unarmed people. Do you remember Biljani school?" You respond: "I heard of the Biljani school. I believe that at that time, I was -- I can't tell you where I was because I may not be right. But I was either on the front line or I was at the assembly. It was only upon my return to Kljuc that I heard that something like that had happened in Biljani." And the Prosecutor says: Yes. There was an another almost identical massacre on the 10th of July at the Biljani school, wasn't there?" And you say: "Yes, that's exactly what I just said."

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this statement of mine in the Brdjanin case can fully be taken as such. I cannot say anything different now, different to what I said then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: In answer to question number 22, Mr. Kalabic, you state that anyone who expressed their wish to leave Kljuc was allowed and enabled to leave. For their own safety they were provided with organised transport and escort to their destination. But it's true, isn't it, that it was the policy of the Kljuc authorities that all Muslims, whether they wanted to leave or not, should be cleansed from the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that is not correct. That was not the policy of the municipality of Kljuc. As a matter of fact, I can refer to Asim Egrlic's statement when he clearly said that the leadership of the SDS in Kljuc was not made up of extremists and one could seek agreement with them. So the Party of Democratic Action, what was it called now? This Muslim Bosniak -- MBO, yes? They pointed out that the Muslim population from the area of the municipality of Kljuc should move out as soon as possible. The leadership of the municipality of Kljuc made every effort not to have this done or, rather, to find a method on the basis of which people would stay on in Kljuc rather than move out. Certain decisions were made along those lines, and if the Prosecution asks me about that I'm going to provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 40138?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This, Mr. Kalabic, is a video.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And I'd like to see -- I'm sorry, it's 40138B. And we are going to watch the footage from 54 minutes onwards.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The political security situation in the Kljuc municipality is quite complicated. We feel free to say that in the last 10 days, the situation has improved somewhat so that the situation is, one can say, calming down. One may say that the topic of some normal life and business is arising and in the future we will secure some normal way of life and business in the territory of the whole municipality provided that certain system, as the economical and public institutions will start functioning normally and life -- "Let me ask you frankly. Do you think that it's possible after all these events that Muslims and Serbs live together in the area of your municipality? "Generally it is difficult to answer this question. I mean, how to assess such a matter. I think that life has to be totally ethnically demarcated and the areas ethnically cleansed of those who cannot live together in this area."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, do you recognise the individual in this video?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise the president of the municipality, Jovo Banjac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And it's true, isn't it, that the policy of Mr. Banjac and the Kljuc authorities was that the area be ethnically cleansed of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: No. That was not the policy of the leadership of the Kljuc municipality at that moment. This was a personal view expressed by Mr. Banjac which was never translated into any kind of official policy of the municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6552, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one very brief matter -- additional matter to deal with, if I could -- if we could move into private session, please, as it relates to a confidential matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, thank you for your indulgence in relation to the additional time. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll be very brief since the Prosecution has taken up quite a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kalabic, you've been shown various statements you made on various occasions here. On those occasions, were the same sorts of questions put to you? Questions that you answered?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that the questions were completely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 52, could you tell us the following: It was suggested that the SDS municipal board was working and you were shown the minutes from the session of the Crisis Staff. Could you tell us whether the Crisis Staff of Kljuc municipality was a party organ or was it a state organ?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of Kljuc municipality was a state organ, and it replaced the work of the Kljuc Municipality Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 57, it was suggested that the Crisis Staff participated in establishing the 17th Light Brigade and providing it with equipment. Can you tell us the name that was used for the 17th Brigade? How was it called?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The 17th Brigade, if that's what you have in mind, was called the Kljuc Brigade, the 17th Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who would take decisions on establishing brigades within our system?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can provide a precise answer to that question but the decisions were certainly not taken by the municipal authorities. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that it relied on the municipality for logistics. According to our law, how is the matter regulated? Is it unlawful, in fact, for area units to cooperate with the local authorities, with the area authorities? How is it from a legal point of view?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: It's not illegal. The local community has to provide logistic support for the army that is on the territory, on its territory, and the command of such a unit is part of the entire command chain of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to the sessions of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Seldom. The president of the municipal board of the SDS usually went there. I was someone -- sometimes there but it was not very frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any sessions that you regularly attended?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I attended sessions of the assembly on a regular basis. Maybe I was absent on some occasions, I can't remember, but if that was the case, it was for family reasons or for other reasons. But one could say that I regularly attended those sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who dealt with the salaries -- or, rather, payments for sleeping over and for the expenses incurred at the Holiday Inn when we were there on an official basis?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I don't know because I usually did not sleep in hotels. I didn't usually stay in hotels. I usually stayed in private flats, at the Ciglane facility in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where did the delegates, representatives, have lunch when we had sessions held in the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it was in the hotel itself or on the premises of the BiH Assembly. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Here we see that on the 15th of February, you were in Sarajevo. That's in 1992. Do you remember whether in addition to the meeting on the 14th of February there was another meeting on the 15th of February?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I can't remember any such event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see P1350 in e-court? Could we please see page 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this 7th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection. The witness has just stated that he didn't remember the meeting of 15 February.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't ask whether he remembered the session of the assembly but does he remember some sort of a meeting on the 17th -- or, rather, on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have to have a look at the document first and then I'll probably be able to answer your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember this agenda. I do remember this assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether you reported to your organs in Kljuc municipality on the session held on the 14th of February, the session of the Main Board, or on the session of the Executive Board on the 15th of February?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I think that my report concerns the session of the assembly that was held on the 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now have a look at the agenda. Is there anything here that was illegal, that was of a delicate nature?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: There is no such thing in the agenda, nothing that would disrupt the regular course of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you present at the session of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you at the session of the Main Board on the 19th of December, 1991, in Sarajevo? The plenary session of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I assume that that was the case, but I would have to refresh my memory by consulting certain documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And during that period of time was some other session held about which you reported?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember that right now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show D86 now? D00086.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber which session these minutes refer to?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: These minutes refer to the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is on page 4, so could we please have a look at page 4 in the Serbian version now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you attended this assembly session?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the previous page in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this agenda and tell us: Is there anything here that has to do with Crisis Staffs or with Variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the agenda in English too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is nothing in the agenda that concerns Variant A and B, and there is nothing that concerns Crisis Staffs either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, did you take any notes of important matters or did you store everything in your memory?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Mostly I tried to remember things. I didn't take many notes. If something was thought to be very important, then I would make a note of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And after you had reported to the municipal organs, did any of them keep the reports you submitted to them?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Well, my reports were very brief, and not particularly expansive, and if there was anything in the minutes of the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency, well, that's all there was. There was nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only have one other question for you. Towards the end of September 1991, when you gave a speech that you have been shown here, well, could you tell us what the circumstances were like, what was going on in Croatia, and what was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: What I can say is that the war was raging in Croatia. On a daily basis the JNA was attacked. It came to a halt to a certain extent and then withdrew to a certain extent. It never really got engaged. That was in Croatia. As I said, in Croatia, they used insignia that reminded us of what happened in 1941. Those insignia and symbols also appeared in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On one occasion, with a group of representatives, we went to Krajina. We travelled to Krajina, and in Vitez we had to go back. We stayed there for two days and, finally, we managed to reach the territory of the Banja Luka municipality through Zenica. We weren't able to get through because that's what the situation was like. There were these people with these insignia and with weapons and they wouldn't allow us to pass through. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were two peoples who outvoted the Serbian people at the assembly, it was a case of majorisation, they issued a declaration, it was a case of outvoting. They mentioned a referendum, holding a referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the Serbian people were outvoted, and as a result, this spread a significant amount of fear, and there were also certain other consequences that were felt in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 28, you were asked about what was happening there and you said that there were victims from the Second World War who had been buried at the cemetery. Where had they been up until that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The victims from the Second World War were buried there earlier on too. I can't remember when this happened but those victims were buried at that cemetery, in that cemetery. And in the former system, the cemetery was always called the partisan cemetery, although no partisans were buried there. The victims of terror spread against the Serbian people in 1941 were buried there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether the events that took place in 1941 and in September 1991 were events that the public was aware of or did the public become aware of these events through your speech?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: On that day, there were several speeches. My speech was referred to because I'm testifying, but there were a number of speakers at that meeting. There were quite a few people who were aware of these things, but no one spoke about these things or no one would speak about those things in public at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my final question now, Mr. Kalabic, is as follows: Whenever you were interviewed, did you ever consciously try to provide various types of answers?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: No, I never tried to provide answers of different kinds, and if there were any divergences, any differences, it's not the essence of my answer that was different. The main reason is that I didn't have the relevant document at hand or it could be because of all the time that has passed and, as a result, not everything can be remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kalabic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Kalabic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it's all right. In lines 2 and 3, he said that if there were any differences, they weren't differences of an important kind, nothing substantially different was said. But I think it's okay. I don't know whether there are any linguistic differences. We could listen to this to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, bring in the next witness. Dobrijevic? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I didn't mean we could listen to this but I thought we were taking care of the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be looked at. I see your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dobrijevic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And make yourself comfortable. As you may know well, Mr. Dobrijevic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal before you commence your evidence. That is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled under such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Dobrijevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Dobrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to make a pause between question and answer and we should speak slowly so that everything can be transcribed. Did you give my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D49040?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see your statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Witness statement, Mile Dobrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read through this statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read through the statement and I did sign it, but there are three minor corrections that I would like to make. They don't change much but it has to do with my status. For example, in paragraph 2, I work in the Special Prosecutor's Office from 2006 not 2009. So it must have been a typing error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is the penultimate line in paragraph 2, so it should say from 2006?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, instead of 2009, 2006. And can I use this statement that I have on me? It concerns another error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will make it easier for me to find my bearings. On page 5, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you like to refer to the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 7. It's paragraph 7, item 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Instead of the name Hadzic, the name or, rather, surname is Avdic. I remembered this later. So the surname Hodzic or Hadzic should be Avdic. Amir Avdic from the territory of Kljuc municipality. And in paragraph 14, item 3, the first sentence, shall I read the entire sentence out? Part of the people taken to Manjaca were not interviewed and I remained here with others on two occasions -- or I, together with the others, on two occasions -- instead of "on two occasions," it should say "on three occasions."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the last page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we say that, with these corrections, the statement faithfully reflects what you've said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the Defence is tendering one associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. And also I would ask that it be added to our 65 ter list as it wasn't on that list and it was just discussed during the proofing when the witness arrived here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Pelic. Do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit both the statement and the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement receives Exhibit Number D4170, Your Honours, and the associated exhibit, D4171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall now read in English a short summary of the statement of Mr. Mile Dobrijevic. [In English] Mile Dobrijevic was an inspector for the crime prevention police in the SJB in Sanski Most. The ethnic composition of the policemen in Sanski Most was proportional to the ethnic composition of the Sanski Most municipality general population. However, the police station was divided on the 6th of April, 1992, as the leadership at the municipal level had agreed to divide the territory of Sanski Most in two municipalities. It was agreed that the Serbian policemen would remain in the SJB and that the Muslims and Croats members could stay with there as well and wear insignia prescribed by the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, most Muslim officers refused to wear the insignias and decided to leave the SJB. Muslim officers forcibly entered the premises of the Municipal Assembly and formed their own SJB. Mile Dobrijevic was aware that the Serbian side took power in Sanski Most peacefully and an offer was made to everyone, regardless of their ethnicity, to stay and live in peace. The Muslims would not leave the Municipal Assembly peacefully. However, they were -- there were no casualties when the Serbian authorities took the building. Once the Muslim SJB had left, weapons and some improvised mines and explosives were found, including 1.000 barrels that had been stuffed with explosives and pieces of scrap iron. Mile Dobrijevic knew that the Muslims were arming illegally, particularly after the results of the plebiscite and, as a result, the SJB began calling people for interviews. From interviews, it was established that the weapons were brought by two Muslims from Germany and Croatia. These weapons were then distributed, and after this, the Muslim side formed its command, companies of men were sent up, and patrol and villages guards were also established. On 25th of May, 1992, the political leadership of Sanski Most made a decision that illegally owned weapons and military equipment should be seized. The SJB were tasked with collecting certain pieces of information and assisting the army in the seizing of illegally owned weapons. A number of people voluntarily surrendered their weapons and military equipment, and following this, the SJB started searching and taking people into custody for -- who failed who respond to the voluntary surrender of weaponry. As early as March 1992, the SJB had information that Muslim women and children were leaving Sanski Most and that able-bodied men were staying behind. Mile Dobrijevic is aware of a collection centre in Sanski Most where Muslims gathered voluntarily as they felt safe and protected, and it was possible for all those who wished to leave Sanski Most to do so, and they were not prevented from leaving. Teams were formed at the public security station level in charge of protecting abandoned property, preventing looting, destruction, and the stealing of movable and immovable property. Serbian refugees were then housed in these properties, and measures and sanctions were put in place against people who unlawfully damaged property. Mile Dobrijevic knows of no civilian authorities at the local or municipal level committing, supporting or ordering the permanent removal through genocide, persecution, extermination, murder, deportation or inhumane acts, all the Muslims and Croats from those territories of BH to which the Serbs laid claim. Mile Dobrijevic that the crisis in the municipality escalated as certain individuals had too many weapons and could not be -- that could not be placed under control in a short space of time. And that's a short summary. Now I will see for some additional documents. Is it embarrassing to stop today five minutes earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that we had a one-hour lunch break, the Chamber is minded to go till 3.00, unless there is a serious opposition.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, I will try to catch up but I have some confusion about documents. It will be resolved soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe we could take a five-minute break. There were some additional exhibits that Dr. Karadzic didn't bring with him. He doesn't have the copies, so they would have to be printed out in order for him to use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees no problem. We'll rise for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, you were a professional policeman and inspector.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the procedure when you found out a murder had been committed? What would you do, which steps would you take, in different cases depending on the ethnicity of the victim and the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Not only murders, but all other crimes would be reported to the duty service, and then men would go on the scene, conduct an on-site investigation, collect clues and other evidence, prepare a record and protocol in order to facilitate the identification of the perpetrator. Not only in the case of murders but all other crimes, aggravated theft, theft, and other offences, policemen would be involved and inspector. If we are talking about murders, there was a crime prevention service that would handle such cases, together with the prosecutor and the investigating judge, because, at that time, the investigating judge would also conduct investigations and would be present at the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, between the question and your answer, please put a pause. Otherwise, the interpreters have difficulties following your answer due to the overlap. So your previous answer to the question whether you were a professional policeman and an inspector was not duly reflected because there was no interpretation. So your answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who reported criminal offences, let's say against Muslims and Croats, if you obtained such information?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We usually found out on the basis of reports from certain persons, or by observing them directly, like any other crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "certain persons"? Did Muslims and Croats come to you to report something that had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, if they had any problems, and if they were not the victims of the crime, or perhaps somebody from the family would come. If we are talking about a murder, then the victim cannot come and report the crime himself or herself, and then we would come out to the scene. Or sometimes it happened that the person was wounded, the victim would go to the medical centre, and the medical centre, the emergency room, would call our public security station and we would go to the medical centre to see what it was all about, and later form a team that would go to the scene, conduct an on-site investigation and take all the steps necessary to identify the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D49033 is the next document I would like to call up in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In which period of the war did it happen, these Muslims and Croats who came to you to report crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: There was no particular period. They reported crimes whenever they could. What do you mean in which period? They reported crimes all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Can you tell us what is this document? You signed it.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Work plan in the detection of the criminal offence of murder, specified in Article 36, murder committed against Hasan Selimovic on 12 July 1995 in a place called Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the ethnicity of the victim?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Hasan Selimovic, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the plan it is envisaged that you check out where his sons were, for a medical examiner to examine the body, on-site investigation, preparing a record, conducting an analysis, et cetera. Was this plan implemented?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the outcome?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The perpetrator was identified. It was Bogdan Ristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Prosecuted? I think he's now serving his sentence. Bogdan Ristic later committed another crime or perhaps it was an attempted murder, but the victim was injured in any case, so he was tried one more time after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the date of this plan?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: 12 July 1995, plan made by Mile Dobrijevic - that's me - and plan approved by chief of section, Slavko Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the population of Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Kijevo was a village with a majority Muslim population. We, the public security station, had a constant presence or kept an eye on that village. But speaking of this incident, this Ristic is also from Kijevo, although he lived on top of a hill overlooking Kijevo, and he targeted people whom he intercepted with his gun. Allegedly, his own son, Ristic's son, had been killed and he was out for a revenge. In any case, he was prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When was he tried, Mr. Ristic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After he was arrested, a criminal report was written and then he was turned over to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking this question because you said he attempted to commit another crime. So he was not arrested because of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not have this knowledge at that time. In the meantime, he attempted another crime so he was later tried for both cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When was he tried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably later, because we see that this is 1995. Ristic is now serving a prison sentence in Bihac. Now, whether he was prosecuted in this period or after the 10th of October, 1995, after we had left Sanski Most, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D4172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have further questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few more documents. If we are going to extend the session, I am willing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer it will take?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15, 20 minutes probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we will continue tomorrow. Mr. Dobrijevic, I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. I take it you understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Hearing is adjourned.
